turns.q: How much room does Exxon have if oil falls? Give net debt to EBITDA, EBIT interest coverage and FCF to debt for the latest four quarters against the same four a year earlier, read what the 10-K says about debt maturities and floating-rate exposure, and relate that to our XOM weight and the book's beta to USO.
turns.answer:
Exxon’s latest-quarter balance-sheet room is decent, but the trend says it has less cushion than a year ago.
On leverage, Exxon’s net debt to EBITDA moved from -0.54× to -0.27×, then -0.09×, and 0.44×. A year earlier, the same quarters were not returned as an aligned series, so I can’t quote the prior-year quarter-by-quarter line from the desk.
Interest coverage was volatile over the same latest four quarters: 72.95×, 120.02×, 49.61×, and 23.64×. FCF to debt fell from 97.2% to 65.8%, 56.2%, and 15.4%. That combination says the company still has room, but the room is shrinking if oil weakens and cash generation stays under pressure.
What the 10-K says supports that caution. The filing explicitly flags that results can move with “global or regional changes or imbalances in the supply and demand for oil, natural gas, petrochemicals, and feedstocks,” “changes in interest and exchange rates,” and “the ability to access debt markets on favorable terms or at all”. That is the desk’s strongest quoted linkage to downside room: lower oil can hit earnings and cash flow, and the company itself says debt-market access and rates matter.
I could not get a quoted passage on debt maturities or floating-rate exposure from the 10-K extract the desk returned. The desk only supplied Item 7 narrative, and it did not provide a maturity schedule or a floating-rate sensitivity table. So on those two points, the evidence is unavailable here, not favorable or unfavorable.
For the book, XOM is 4.61% of port_001. The book beta to USO was not returned; the desk could only give XOM’s beta to SPY, which was -0.56×. That means I cannot tie the portfolio’s oil beta directly to USO from the evidence in hand. What I can say is that XOM is a mid-sized single-name weight, so a weaker oil tape would matter to the book through that position, but the desk did not provide the book-level USO beta needed to quantify the portfolio’s oil sensitivity.

turns.q: Compare the capex intensity and ROIC of Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon over the last three fiscal years. Who spends the most relative to revenue and earns the least on it, and how does that sit with the book's exposure to QQQ?
turns.answer:
On the evidence shown, Amazon spends the most relative to revenue and earns the least on that spending. Its capex was "$132B" against revenue of "$717B" for the latest fiscal year shown, and its ROIC was "16.2%". By comparison, Microsoft had capex of "$64.55B" on revenue of "$282B" and ROIC of "29.7%", while Alphabet had capex of "$91.45B" on revenue of "$350B" and ROIC of "24.8%". Over the last three fiscal years, the direction is the same in the series the desk showed: Microsoft capex rose from "$28.11B" to "$44.48B" to "$64.55B"; Alphabet from "$32.25B" to "$52.53B" to "$91.45B"; Amazon from "$52.73B" to "$83.00B" to "$132B". ROIC over the same span was "32.8%", "29.7%", "29.7%" for Microsoft; "26.8%", "25.2%", "26.6%", "29.7%", "24.8%" for Alphabet; and "15.2%", "22.3%", "16.2%" for Amazon.
For the book, the relevant holdings are already there: MSFT is "16.0%", GOOGL is "12.4%", and AMZN is "7.03%". The book also has sector exposure to Communication_Services at "12.4%" and Consumer_Discretionary at "7.03%", but there is no QQQ exposure held in the desk’s portfolio figures shown, so I cannot say the book is directly exposed to QQQ. What I can say is that the book is materially exposed to the same mega-cap growth complex that dominates QQQ through MSFT, GOOGL and AMZN. That makes the capex-heavy, lower-ROIC profile of Amazon the main capital-allocation drag among these names, while Microsoft looks strongest on ROIC and least stretched on capex intensity, with Alphabet in between. What the desk could show is that net margin has already moved up a lot: 26.2% [f_c8ce64f1a27f@2024-06-30], 8.48% [f_c8ce64f1a27f@2024-09-30], 32.6% [f_c8ce64f1a27f@2024-12-31], 21.7% [f_c8ce64f1a27f@2025-03-31], 36.4% [f_c8ce64f1a27f@2025-06-30], 31.7% [f_c8ce64f1a27f@2025-09-30], 34.4% [f_c8ce64f1a27f@2025-12-31], and 37.4% [f_c8ce64f1a27f@2026-03-31]. That is a strong level, but not a monotonic trend; it has been volatile.

The earnings bridge is supportive, but not unambiguous. Revenue rose to $19.80B [f_226e3b6b4dc1@2026-03-31] from $11.30B [f_226e3b6b4dc1@2024-06-30], while cost of revenue rose to $3.58B [f_21e72ec3a985@2026-03-31] from $2.17B [f_21e72ec3a985@2024-06-30]. Net income rose to $7.40B [f_147d744cd502@2026-03-31] from $2.97B [f_147d744cd502@2024-06-30], and operating cash flow rose to $5.33B [f_6d6abc177682@2026-03-31] from $1.47B [f_6d6abc177682@2024-06-30]. But the cost line has also been accelerating: cost of revenue was $2.45B [f_21e72ec3a985@2025-06-30], $3.01B [f_21e72ec3a985@2025-09-30], $3.37B [f_21e72ec3a985@2025-12-31], and $3.58B [f_21e72ec3a985@2026-03-31]. That means margin expansion is still being tested by rising cost growth.

Management’s own filing points to the core driver: “Net income and earnings per share increased in 2025, primarily due to higher gross margin, partially offset by increased marketing, selling, and administrative expenses and research and development expenses.” It also says revenue increased “primarily by increased volume, partially offset by lower realized prices,” driven by Mounjaro and Zepbound. That is margin-positive if volume keeps outrunning mix and pricing pressure, but the filing does not give a forecast, and it explicitly flags offsets from spending.

So the implication for the book is: the margin story is still constructive, but next year’s expansion is not something the desk can assert. The evidence supports “can keep expanding if volume and gross margin continue to outrun SG&A and R&D,” not “will keep expanding.” The main thing that would change that reading is either evidence of sustained gross-margin improvement with controlled expense growth, or evidence that pricing pressure and operating expense growth are catching up."}
